title: Heidegger and Merleau-Ponty
summary: Phenomenology is a philosophy that tries to describe experience as it is lived from the inside, rather than explain it “from the outside.” Heidegger explored how a person always already lives in the world, cares about it and is attuned to it; Merleau-Ponty showed that this experience is bodily from the very start: we don't “have” a body, we are the body through which we have a world.
onEmotions: For Heidegger, feelings are not “inner states” locked up in the head but “attunement” (Befindlichkeit): the way the world is always already disclosed to us, before any reflection. We are never “out of mood” — even flat indifference is a mood. So a feeling doesn't distort reality; it shows us something about it. Merleau-Ponty adds that feeling lives in the body — in breath, posture, gesture — and that this is not an obstacle to understanding but its first, bodily form.

anxiety.text: In a 1929 lecture Heidegger said that anxiety “leaves us hanging”: everything slips away, with nothing to hold on to. If that's how you're swaying right now, it isn't a malfunction. Heidegger distinguished fear from anxiety (Angst): fear is always directed at something definite, while anxiety is directed at nothing in particular. In it, the familiar world seems to lose its weight, and a person is left alone with the fact that their life is theirs alone and no one else will live it for them. So anxiety can be not only muffled but also listened to: often it tells you that other people's “generally accepted” answers no longer fit you. Merleau-Ponty would add that anxiety lives in the body — in your breath, in your shoulders — and that this too is a way of being in the world, not a mistake.
anxiety.practice: For a minute, “bracket” the question “how do I get rid of this?” and describe the anxiety out loud, the way a phenomenologist describes a thing: where it is in your body, what it's like, where it pulls. Then ask: what has stopped being self-evident for me?

fear.text: In the face of what, about what, and what is the fearing itself? — Heidegger split fear into these three questions. If you're frightened, there's no shame in it — ask them. For Heidegger, fear is one kind of attunement: it is always fear “in the face of” something approaching and threatening, and fear “about” something. That is its honesty: you can only be afraid for what matters to you. Heidegger called this basic feature of human beings “care” (Sorge): something always matters to us; we can't be truly indifferent to our own lives. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that fear is bodily first: the body “knows” about danger before thought does, and it tenses to protect you. To accept fear is to see in it not cowardice but a form of care, and to ask what exactly it is caring about right now.
fear.practice: Say out loud: “I'm afraid for…” — and listen to what comes after the dots. For Heidegger, it will be something you care about.

sadness.text: Heidegger might have compared a mood to the weather: we don't choose it, we find ourselves already inside it. If you're sad even without a clear reason, there is nothing wrong in that. For Heidegger we are never “without a mood”: even grey indifference is a mood. A mood, he wrote, comes neither from outside nor from inside but rises out of our very “being-in-the-world”; we don't choose it, we find ourselves in it. So sadness is not a dark pane of glass between you and reality, but one of the ways reality discloses itself at all: in sadness, fragility, silence and what is passing become more visible. Merleau-Ponty would show how sadness changes perception itself: colours fade, steps grow heavy, the world seems to recede. Sadness doesn't have to be fixed urgently — you can let it show you what it sees.
sadness.practice: Look around for a minute through the eyes of your sadness, fixing nothing: what do you notice now — fragility, silence, what is passing — that you usually don't see?

grief.text: After the death of someone close, for Heidegger, we don't part with them but stay nearby — “dwelling with them in mourning and remembrance,” as Being and Time puts it. Your grief is one of the deepest human attunements, and it needs no justification. The one who is gone hasn't simply vanished: they are still part of your world — that shared world which, for Heidegger, we always inhabit with others (he called this “being-with,” Mitsein). Hence the pain: the world is being rearranged, and familiar paths lead to an empty place. Merleau-Ponty would add that the body remembers: hands, habits, everyday routes keep the presence of the one who is gone. Grief is not an illness but a form of faithfulness to a bond. It doesn't need to be “got through faster”; the world can rearrange itself slowly, keeping a place for what was lost.
grief.practice: Walk slowly along one of the routes you used to share — to the shop, across the yard, down a corridor — and let your body remember. Merleau-Ponty would say the body keeps the presence of the one who is gone.

loneliness.text: From his hut in the Black Forest Heidegger wrote that solitude does not isolate us but casts our whole existence into the vast nearness of all things. Loneliness still hurts, but there's nothing shameful in it. Heidegger held that human beings are essentially “being-with” (Mitsein): we always already live in a world shared with others. So, as he saw it, even loneliness is a particular way of being with others: you can only miss someone who in principle could be there. Your loneliness isn't proof that you're built “wrong” but evidence that you're made for connection. Merleau-Ponty spoke of “intercorporeality” — the way bodies understand one another even before words: through a glance, a gesture, an intonation. Perhaps loneliness is the body's longing for this kind of living response. To accept it is to hear in it not a verdict but a direction.
loneliness.practice: Today, meet someone's eyes a little longer than usual — a shop assistant, a neighbour, a passer-by — and smile. Merleau-Ponty would call it intercorporeality: bodies understand each other before words.

anger.text: A phenomenologist would ask not “why am I angry?” but “how does the world appear to me right now?” Anger is a living feeling, and it often speaks of something important. Heidegger hardly wrote about anger directly, but if we extend his analysis of attunement, in anger, the world appears as something that affects us, that “concerns” us. What is indifferent to us doesn't make us angry; so anger, too, is a form of “care.” Merleau-Ponty would draw attention to the body: anger isn't a thought to which sensations were later added, but a whole way of being in a situation — tension, heat, readiness to act. The body “understood” what was happening as a violation before you had time to put it into words. To accept anger is not to be ashamed of it but to ask: what boundary, what value is it protecting right now?
anger.practice: Place your palm where you feel the anger most strongly in your body and ask: “What matters to me here?”

shame.text: The body, Merleau-Ponty noticed, both sees and is seen: at any moment we may find ourselves under someone else's gaze. Everyone knows the moment when that gaze suddenly burns. Shame is the moment when the body suddenly feels exposed, turned into an object, and you want to disappear. Heidegger would add the concept of “das Man” — the impersonal “they,” “the done thing”: often we're ashamed not before a specific person but before an anonymous “that's not how it's done.” It's worth asking: whose standard is this — your own, or “people in general”? Shame doesn't make you worse; it shows how much it matters to you to be among others. And sometimes it's enough to notice that this gaze is not yet the whole world.
shame.practice: Picture the person you feel ashamed before, concretely — a face, a name. Now try to picture “what people will say”: that voice has no face. Heidegger called it “das Man” — no one and everyone at once.

guilt.text: The “call of conscience,” for Heidegger, calls in silence: it lists nothing, accuses no one, and simply brings a person back to their own life. Guilt is heavy, but it doesn't make you a bad person. Heidegger distinguished everyday guilt — a debt, a wrongdoing — from a deeper “being-guilty” (Schuldigsein), which, as he saw it, belongs to human beings as such. In choosing one thing, we inevitably don't choose another; we can't do everything, and we never begin with a clean slate. To be human is to be finite and always to fall short somewhere. This is not a verdict but a release from the illusion of flawlessness. You can listen to guilt, put right what really can be put right, and let go of the demand to be infinite.
guilt.practice: Sit in silence for a minute and listen for the wordless “call”: not “what did I do wrong?” but “what life of mine is this guilt calling me back to?” Then put right one thing that really can be put right.

envy.text: “Everyone is the other, and no one is himself” — that is how Heidegger described life in the impersonal “das Man.” When envy stings, we are looking at ourselves through other people's eyes. Heidegger described everyday life as absorption in “das Man” — the impersonal “they”: we constantly compare ourselves, find out how “everyone” lives and measure ourselves by other people's yardsticks. He called this “distantiality” (Abständigkeit) — a quiet, almost imperceptible preoccupation with the distance between ourselves and others. Envy is a sign that for a while you're seeing your own life through someone else's eyes. But it also holds a clue: envy points to what you want. Heidegger spoke of “authenticity” (Eigentlichkeit) — a life you understand as your own, not as a copy of a common template. Then envy becomes not a reproach but a question: what do I want — not “they”?
envy.practice: Say out loud what you envy, and rephrase it: “I would like…”. Is this wish yours — or “theirs”?

emptiness.text: Heidegger once looked long at an ordinary jug and concluded that it holds not by its walls or base but by its emptiness: the void is what receives and keeps. If you feel empty and drained right now, that thought may be unexpectedly gentle. Heidegger described moments when things stop calling to us and meaning anything, and everything “becomes indifferent.” For him such states are not just a glitch: in them something usually hidden shows through — that the world as a whole rests on our involvement. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that meaning is born in the body and in movement, in the simplest gestures. Sometimes the way out of emptiness begins not with a big idea but with a small bodily contact with the world: a warm cup, footsteps, a sound. Emptiness is not a final answer but a world that has gone quiet for a while.
emptiness.practice: Pour water or tea into a cup and hold it in your palms, looking at the emptiness that holds. Stay with that warmth for half a minute, demanding nothing of yourself.

confusion.text: Holzwege, “Forest Paths” — Heidegger named a book after the woodcutters' tracks that break off in the thicket: those who know understand what it means to be on such a path. If you're confused, you're on one — an honest reaction to a world that has stopped making sense. Heidegger described how we usually live “absorbed in our dealings”: things are “ready-to-hand” (zuhanden) for us — we use them without thinking, like a hammer in the hand. Only when something breaks does the thing suddenly become noticeable and strange. Confusion is like such a breakdown of the familiar: what used to work “by itself” has stopped working. It's unpleasant, but that's exactly when the very structure of your life, usually invisible, comes into view. Confusion is not a failure but a moment when you can take a fresh look at what matters to you.
confusion.practice: Go for a short walk with no goal or route — let it be your own “forest path.” On the way, name to yourself one thing that has stopped working “by itself,” without looking for a solution yet.

fatigue.text: Heidegger gazed at Van Gogh's painted shoes: from their dark, worn insides, he wrote, stares the toil of the worker's tread. If you're exhausted, your body speaks that same language. Merleau-Ponty showed that the body is not a tool operated by the mind but our way of being in the world: it is through the body that we have a world at all. At the root of our experience he saw a bodily “I can” — the ability to reach, to walk, to take something on. When the body is tired, the world literally changes: distances grow longer, tasks heavier, “I can” turns into “I can't.” Fatigue is not an enemy to defeat but a signal of your embodied existence: you are not a machine, and your world may shrink for a while so that you can recover.
fatigue.practice: Ask your body, not your mind: “What do you want right now?” — and note the first answer, even if it's very simple.

quote.text: I am not in front of my body, I am in it, or rather I am it.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

boredom.text: A station on a sleepy branch line, four hours until the train, and you count the trees along the road and keep checking your watch — Heidegger began his famous analysis of boredom with this scene. He devoted much of his course The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1929–1930) to this seemingly trivial theme. He distinguished superficial boredom — as at that station — from “profound boredom,” when everything at once becomes indifferent, including ourselves. In profound boredom time seems to stand still, and we find ourselves facing what we usually drown out with constant busyness. For Heidegger this is not a waste of life but one of the “fundamental moods,” which can awaken a question: what do I actually want to live for? Boredom doesn't have to be filled with something right away. You can give it a little space — and see what it opens up.
boredom.practice: Next time you're bored, wait two minutes before picking up your phone. What surfaces in that pause?

quote.text: Profound boredom, drifting here and there in the abysses of our existence like a muffling fog, removes all things and human beings and oneself along with them into a remarkable indifference.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

joy.text: In Freiburg in 1929, in a lecture about the Nothing and anxiety, Heidegger suddenly spoke of joy — joy in the presence of someone we love: in it, he said, “beings as a whole” are revealed. Your joy is as real a knowledge of the world as anxiety. In other words, joy is not a superficial emotion but a way in which the world suddenly appears whole, close and open. Merleau-Ponty would show how joy changes the body: it becomes light, movements become free, everything seems within reach. This is the bodily “I can” at its fullest. To accept joy is not to devalue it with thoughts like “this won't last” or “I don't deserve it,” but to let it be a full experience of the world. Joy needs no justification and doesn't have to “pay for itself.”
joy.practice: Where in your body do you feel joy? Keep your attention there for three calm breaths — just so the joy is noticed.

love.text: A bridge, Heidegger wrote, doesn't just connect banks that are already there: the banks first emerge as banks when the bridge crosses the stream. Tenderness is a bridge like that, one of the deepest ways of being with another. Speaking of “caring for another” (Fürsorge), Heidegger distinguished two extreme forms. One, as it were, leaps in and takes over the other's concerns, quietly making them dependent. The other “leaps ahead” of them — and gives their own care back to them, helping them become themselves. Mature tenderness is closer to the second, liberating form. Merleau-Ponty would show that love begins in the body: in a touch, the one “touching” and the one “touched” intertwine, and the boundary between “I” and “you” becomes permeable. To love is to be vulnerable, and there's no weakness in that.
love.practice: When you touch someone close today — a hand on the shoulder, a hug — linger a second longer and notice how “touching” and “touched” intertwine. Ask yourself: does my care help them be themselves?

gratitude.text: Denken ist Danken — “to think is to thank”: the late Heidegger made this play on German words a key to his lectures What Is Called Thinking? (1951–1952). The gratitude you feel right now is, as he saw it, an attentive receiving of what is given to us. It is not a polite formula but a way of seeing: things are not to be taken for granted; they are given to us. Merleau-Ponty would add that we receive the world from the very start — through the body, perception, language, other people — before we ever do anything ourselves. Gratitude, then, is an acknowledgement of our rootedness in the world. It doesn't have to be earned or turned into a debt; you can simply let it be.
gratitude.practice: Name one thing in today that you usually take for granted, and say to yourself: “This was given to me.”

hope.text: “Potentiality-for-being” (Seinkönnen) — that is how Heidegger understood a person: not a set of fixed properties but an open space of what they may yet become. If you hope even when a lot is unclear, you are living in that very space. Heidegger believed human beings are by nature directed forward: he called this “being-ahead-of-itself.” We always already live in our possibilities, not only in what is here now. He also wrote about the finitude of life — but for him the understanding that time is not endless makes life not less valuable but more: it brings us back to what really matters. Hope is an expression of the fact that you are a being of possibilities. You can cherish it without demanding guarantees from it.
hope.practice: Three times, say out loud: “I am someone for whom it is still possible to…” — and finish it differently each time, even in the smallest way.

nostalgia.text: A smell, a tune or a taste suddenly brings back a whole world — Merleau-Ponty saw bodily memory in this, not just thought. A tender ache for the past says a lot about you, and there's no reason to be ashamed of it. Heidegger emphasised that for a human being the past is not simply what has gone and finished. He called it “having-been-ness” (Gewesenheit): our past goes on living in us and shapes how we see the present and what we expect from the future. We are “thrown” into a history, a language, a family, traditions, and we carry them with us. Nostalgia is not an escape from life but a meeting with what made you. You can accept it as a grateful look back from which to draw strength.
nostalgia.practice: Find one smell, taste or sound from that time today — a tea, a song, a soap — and let your body remember. What from that world would you like to take into today?

craving.text: In Being and Time Heidegger briefly examined “urge” and “addiction” (Drang, Hang) as modifications of care — and noticed that in them the world narrows: of all possibilities only one remains, and it seems to pull you towards itself. A sharp “I want it right now” is nothing to be ashamed of: this is how the body and habit pull us towards a familiar relief. Merleau-Ponty would add that a craving lives in the body before thought: the hand, the breath, the gaze are already turned towards the object. So a craving is not your “true desire” and not a verdict, but a wave of bodily attunement. Like any attunement, it rises, peaks and changes. You can notice it without arguing with it or giving in straight away — and watch the world gradually widen again.
craving.practice: Describe the craving as a bodily sensation: where is it in your body, what is it like — warm, tight, pulsing? Watch for a couple of minutes how its strength changes and how the world slowly widens again.

addiction.text: A typist doesn't remember where the letters are on the keyboard — her fingers know: for Merleau-Ponty, habit is knowledge that lives in the body. So addiction is not a moral failure or a “weakness of character.” In the same way, a long-standing cycle of addiction becomes written into the body, into the daily routine, into routes, into what an evening or a Friday looks like. Heidegger would probably add that the whole world becomes “attuned” around one thing: objects and hours take on meaning in relation to it. This explains why getting out is so hard: it isn't one habit that changes but a whole world. But hope follows from the same thought: since the body once learned, it can also relearn — slowly, through repetition, with the support of others. It's a path, not a single decision.
addiction.practice: Note one place or time of day that is especially “attuned” to the familiar cycle, and rearrange the smallest thing in it. If you like, tell someone about it — someone close, or a mutual-help group.

hangover.text: A phenomenologist would ask: how does the world appear to you right now — and how much of that colour comes from your body rather than the truth about you? Your body aches, anxiety, shame and fragments of the evening rise up, and all of it deserves gentleness, not a verdict. Merleau-Ponty showed that in ordinary life the body is “transparent”: we live through it without noticing — we look with our eyes, not at them. In a hangover the body suddenly comes to the foreground — heavy, alien, demanding attention — and the world around seems dull and prickly too. Heidegger would remind us that attunement colours everything at once — last night, yourself and the future. The morning gloom is not the final truth about you but a mood that will pass. Meanwhile, you can simply look after the body that is so noticeable right now.
hangover.practice: Step out into the fresh air for a couple of minutes and feel your body becoming “transparent” again, if only for a few steps: the ground underfoot, the air on your face.

euphoria.text: Heidegger wrote that an “elated mood” lifts from us the burden of being — the load we usually carry without noticing. A burst in which everything seems attainable right now is a real experience, and there's no need to suspect it straight away. In such moments the world opens up differently: distances shrink, everything seems attainable, the future wide open. For a phenomenologist this is not an illusion but one of the ways the world can be given to us at all. Merleau-Ponty would add that the high is felt in the body: lightness in movement, fast speech, the wish to embrace everything at once. Understanding this is useful not to spoil the moment but to live it attentively: to remember how the world looks in this light, and to notice which of the possibilities that have opened up you'll still want to test on a calm morning.
euphoria.practice: Write in one line how the world looks in this light and what seems possible. Reread it later, in an ordinary mood — like a phenomenologist comparing two ways the world can be given.

crash.text: A mood, Heidegger said, can't be switched off by an act of will — it can only be replaced by another, counter-mood. When the high has gone, the drop can be very hard, and it isn't your fault. Heidegger wrote that in our moods the “burdensome” character of existence is disclosed to us one way or another: life has to be carried. An elated mood lifts this burden for a while but doesn't cancel it; when the high goes, the weight is felt more sharply, by contrast. What matters is that the crash, too, is an attunement, not the final truth about the world. And that comes not through force but through the body and simple tasks. Merleau-Ponty would remind us: the world comes back to us through movement — a step, a breath, a look out of the window.
crash.practice: Without demanding a lift from yourself, make one simple movement — stretch, walk around the room, open a window — and notice what has changed, even by one percent.

panic.text: Merleau-Ponty showed that we find ourselves first of all through the body: the support of our feet, the position of our hands, the boundaries of our skin. When your heart pounds and your breath falters, that support seems to slip away. This fear is real, and you're not exaggerating anything. Heidegger described how in intense fear a person “loses their head”: attention darts from one thing to another, holding on to nothing, and the familiar world seems to fall apart. So the phenomenological answer is simple and bodily: don't argue with your thoughts, but bring the world back to yourself through the body — through what you can feel and name. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes; a body that feels the floor underfoot helps you wait it out.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and press your palms against your knees — give yourself back the boundaries of your body. Take a few breaths with the exhale longer than the inhale, and name out loud five objects you can see.

dread.text: “Why are there beings at all, rather than nothing?” — Heidegger ended his lecture “What Is Metaphysics?” with this question, saying that it arises precisely when, in anxiety, everything slips away. If the question “what's the point of it all?” has hit you and the abyss of finitude is in view, it's one of the hardest experiences there is. Heidegger didn't consider it a sickness of the mind. He also stressed that knowing our finitude makes life truly our own. Since time is not endless, every “now” has weight and won't come again. Dread is the other side of wonder that the world and you exist at all. This question doesn't need to be solved tonight. You can let it be — and notice that you're asking it as someone alive, in a living world.
dread.practice: Find one thing near you that is astonishing simply because it exists: light, a sound, your own breathing. Look at it for a minute, as if asking it Heidegger's question.

fomo.text: Long before social media, Heidegger described “curiosity” (Neugier) — an urge to see the new for the sake of novelty, which jumps from one thing to the next and never lingers: being everywhere and nowhere at once. When the feed shows others living more vividly and you seem to be in the wrong place, it wears you out. And “idle talk” (Gerede) creates the feeling that everyone already knows where real life is, and it's somewhere out there. This is the anonymous voice of “the they” (das Man) — not anyone's specific opinion but an impersonal “this is how people live.” FOMO is not a sign that your life is worse but a trace of a scattered gaze. Its opposite is lingering: life happens where you actually are.
fomo.practice: Choose one thing near you and linger on it for two minutes — look at it as if for the first time. What did you notice that you hadn't seen before?

sleepless.text: I lie down, close my eyes, breathe slowly, imitating a sleeper — and at some point sleep “comes,” as the god appeared to those who enacted his mysteries: that is how Merleau-Ponty, in the Phenomenology of Perception, described falling asleep. Insomnia and three-in-the-morning thoughts are exhausting, and being annoyed with yourself only adds weight. Sleep can't be seized by will; it can only be invited by the body. And night-time thoughts, from Heidegger's point of view, can be understood as a particular attunement: in the dark, when nothing can be done, the world shrinks to worries, and each one seems huge. In the morning the same thought often weighs something different. So there's no need to argue with night-time conclusions — it's enough not to take them as final and to let the body play the part of the sleeper.
sleepless.practice: Lie down comfortably and “play” a sleeper: relax your face, slow your breathing, make the exhale longer. Don't wait for sleep — just play the part.

betrayal.text: A working hammer goes unnoticed, Heidegger observed: it “disappears” into the work and stands out only when it breaks. Trust works the same way, which is why betrayal wounds so deeply, and why the pain makes sense. Heidegger wrote that we always already live in a world shared with others (Mitsein), and much of this world rests on the “taken for granted” — on trust we don't notice, the way we don't notice the floor under our feet. Betrayal wounds more than feelings: it breaks this unnoticed background, and suddenly everything familiar is called into question — past conversations, shared memories, your own capacity to trust. Merleau-Ponty would add that trust is bodily: it lives in relaxed shoulders next to a person, in the habit of turning towards them. Your bewilderment is not naivety but evidence of how genuine your openness was.
betrayal.practice: Name one person or one place where your trust is still intact. Stay for a minute with this feeling of support.

jealousy.text: Even the person closest to us, for Merleau-Ponty, is given to us from one side only — like a house you can never see from all sides at once. Jealousy is agonising, and very many people know it. I see their face and gestures, hear their words, but their world, their perception, their life from the inside I can never live for them. This isn't a flaw in the relationship but the very condition of encounter: the other is not an object but a different point of view on the world. Jealousy can be understood as a painful encounter with this irremovable separateness: you want the person you love to have no side hidden from you. There's no need to be ashamed of jealousy: it carries a longing for closeness — and the pain of knowing that closeness doesn't cancel the other's freedom.
jealousy.practice: Recall a moment when someone close to you revealed an unexpected side of themselves — and it was good. Let yourself notice that their separateness can also bring joy.

resentment.text: Merleau-Ponty noticed that the past settles in the body: in a clenched jaw at the sound of a name, in wariness, in habitual protective gestures. An old grievance is heavy, you carry it for years — and that means something truly mattered to you. Heidegger believed the past doesn't stay behind us like a station we've passed: we are our “having-been” (Gewesenheit); it keeps sounding in the present and in how we await the future. Resentment is the past that has stayed present because the wound was never acknowledged. So you don't have to force yourself to “let it go.” To begin with, you can acknowledge it and notice where it lives in your body. Pain that has been acknowledged gradually stops being the only way of remembering.
resentment.practice: Recall the grievance and ask yourself: where is it in my body right now? Place your palm there and take a few calm breaths out.

heartbreak.text: A person who has lost an arm goes on feeling it for a long time: Merleau-Ponty explained the “phantom limb” by the body still being directed towards a world in which that arm was needed. A broken heart is just as real a pain, and there's no need to be ashamed of its strength. A break-up can be understood the same way. Your body and your habits still live in the shared world: your hand reaches for the phone, your eyes look for a familiar silhouette, your evening is still arranged for two out of habit. That's why a break-up hurts for so long: the world doesn't rearrange itself in a day. This isn't “clinging to the past” but the slow work of a body and a world learning to live anew.
heartbreak.practice: Notice one habit that is still “waiting” for the other person. Don't scold yourself for it — just gently name it: “my body still remembers.”

impostor.text: Cézanne doubted every canvas to the end of his life — Merleau-Ponty wrote a whole essay, “Cézanne's Doubt,” about it. If you feel you're about to be found out, you're in good company: this fear mostly visits the conscientious. Heidegger described the anonymous authority of “the they” (das Man): “this is how it's done,” “this is what's expected,” “real professionals don't make mistakes like that.” No one in particular stands behind this voice, but we measure ourselves by it without meaning to. Impostor syndrome can be understood as comparing yourself from the inside — with all your doubts — to faceless “them” on the outside, who seemingly have no doubts. Merleau-Ponty would add that skill lives in the body and in practice, not in a feeling of confidence: your hands often know more than your head is ready to admit.
impostor.practice: Right now, do something small that you know how to do — with your hands, not in your head: type a paragraph, fix something, cook. Notice how your hands know more than your head is ready to admit.

self_hatred.text: A phenomenologist would ask about the inner critic: whose voice is it speaking in? When that voice is merciless, you deserve gentleness, not yet another verdict. Heidegger has the concept of “the call of conscience,” and it helps to distinguish something important. The genuine call, for Heidegger, lists nothing and brands no one: it silently calls a person to their own possibilities, to being themselves. He considered the everyday understanding of conscience as a ledger of wrongdoings a distortion of it. And the voice that insists “you're worthless” more often speaks the language of “the they” (das Man) — other people's yardsticks, judgements and comparisons, absorbed at some point. It is loud, but it isn't your deepest voice. Its verdict is not the truth about you. Beneath it there is another, quiet call — not to punishment, but to life.
self_hatred.practice: Say one of your inner critic's sentences out loud and ask: “Whose voice is saying this? Where have I heard it before?” Then stay silent for a minute and listen for the other, quiet call.

helplessness.text: “I can” — Merleau-Ponty's name for the very ground of consciousness, deeper than any “I think.” When it seems nothing depends on you, that “can” shrinks to a point, and it is very hard. Heidegger spoke of “thrownness” (Geworfenheit): we always already find ourselves in a situation we didn't choose — in a body, in a history, in circumstances. This is not your fault but a shared human condition. Merleau-Ponty described the body as a primary “I can”: the world for us is a field of what we can reach, what we can pick up, where we can go. But it doesn't vanish completely: even in the tightest situation something remains within reach — straightening a pillow, opening a window, writing one word. You don't have to change everything at once. You can begin by giving your body back at least a small “I can.”
helplessness.practice: Find one very small action within arm's reach and do it slowly, noticing: “I managed that.”

procrastination.text: Merleau-Ponty's patient Schneider couldn't point to his nose on command, yet easily scratched it when a mosquito bit. If you can't get started, it's similar: the head gives an order and the body doesn't respond — and it almost never comes down to laziness. Heidegger observed that we understand the world first of all not with an observer's eyes but in dealing with things: a tool is truly understood when you work with it, not when you think about it. Merleau-Ponty would add that the body understands a task once it starts moving: fingers on the keyboard, an open notebook, a tool in your hand already suggest the next step. You can begin not with resolve but with touch: not “do everything,” but simply pick the thing up. Understanding often comes along the way.
procrastination.practice: Without starting the work, just prepare it with your body: open the file, put the pen on the page, pick up the tool. Stay like that for a minute — with no obligation to go on.

uprooted.text: An organist, Merleau-Ponty wrote, needs only an hour to get used to an unfamiliar organ: hands and feet learn anew where everything is. After a move you have to learn everything at once, and the ground seems to slip from under your feet — this is no whim. Merleau-Ponty showed that space for us is not a map but a lived-in world: the body knows where the light switch is, how to get to the shop, how your native language sounds. Heidegger thought a great deal about “dwelling” (Wohnen): for him, to live is not just to be somewhere but to inhabit a place with care. Your sense of being lost is not a failure but an honest response to the loss of a lived-in world. Home is not just an address: it grows again out of habits, routes and people.
uprooted.practice: Choose one small spot in the new place — a bench, a café, a route — and start returning to it. Feeling at home begins with repetition.

quote.text: Homelessness is coming to be the destiny of the world.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

overload.text: The Rhine, Heidegger wrote, is no longer the river of Hölderlin's poems for technology, but a supplier of hydroelectric power. When the endless feed wears you out, it's not that you're “not coping.” The late Heidegger wrote about “enframing” (Gestell) — an arrangement of the technological world in which everything, including human beings and their attention, becomes a resource to be used. A stream of notifications is a good illustration: it demands a reaction constantly. Yet in his address “Releasement” (Gelassenheit) he proposed saying both “yes” and “no” to technical things at once: using them, but not letting them take hold of us entirely. Being tired of the noise is a healthy response: something in you resists being turned into a resource. You can allow yourself small islands of releasement, where things once again mean something in themselves.
overload.practice: Put your phone face down for two minutes and look at one thing in the room as if it didn't need to be photographed or rated.

unreality.text: “The world is not what I think, but what I live through,” Merleau-Ponty wrote in the preface to the Phenomenology of Perception. When everything around you, or you yourself, seems unreal, it's strange and frightening, and hard to put into words. Merleau-Ponty called our ordinary certainty about the world “perceptual faith”: before any proof, we live with the sense that things exist, that they're solid and real. This faith rests not on logic but on the body — so sometimes it can weaken, as if a pane of glass had appeared between you and the world. Phenomenology begins precisely where what is usually unnoticed becomes noticeable: an experience like this, however hard, shows how finely woven our connection with the world is. Merleau-Ponty stressed that this connection lives in sensation — in touch, weight, temperature, sound. The world answers the body before it answers the mind.
unreality.practice: Pick up an object with a distinct texture — a cool cup, a rough piece of fabric — and describe out loud to yourself its weight, temperature and surface.

awe.text: A Greek temple, Heidegger wrote, stands on the rock and withstands the storm — and in doing so first makes the storm visible in all its violence. Awe before mountains, the sea, the night sky or music is the same kind of showing of the world, and one of the most precious experiences. Heidegger considered wonder one of the original moods from which thought itself is born: the Greeks already said that philosophy begins in wonder. In awe the world is not simply perceived but appears in all its unexpected givenness — as if it were being shown for the first time. Merleau-Ponty saw the task of philosophy as giving us back this fresh gaze, hidden behind habit. Awe is not fleeting sentimentality but a moment when seeing becomes clear. You can simply allow yourself to have it.
awe.practice: Stay with whatever filled you with awe for another minute, without photographing or describing it. Just let it be bigger than you.

quote.text: True philosophy consists in relearning to look at the world.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

relief.text: Only when the weight is lifted can you see how much you were carrying — that's how a phenomenologist would describe this moment. It is one of the most blessed sensations, and it's worth living through without hurrying. Every mood, for Heidegger, discloses the world in its own way, and relief does so especially tellingly. The world becomes spacious again, the future open. Merleau-Ponty would draw attention to the body: relief is almost always bodily — the shoulders drop, the breath deepens, the face smooths out. This is the body returning to a world from which tension had pushed it out. So relief is not a trifle after which you must rush straight on, but a moment when body and world find each other again. Let it last: notice it while it's here.
relief.practice: Notice where in your body you feel the relief — in your shoulders, your breathing, your belly. Take one slow breath out, as if confirming: “yes, it's easier now.”

calm.text: An old oak, a wooden bench, the changing seasons and a path across the fields that Heidegger had walked since childhood — that is what his short text “The Pathway” (1949) is about. The calm you feel right now doesn't need to be earned or justified. Such a path, he wrote, teaches something simple — what remains when the bustle dies down. For Heidegger, calm is not emptiness or inaction but a special openness: things stop being tasks and become simply things again. Merleau-Ponty would add that calm is felt in the body as agreement with the rhythm of the world: breath falls in with your step, your gaze is in no hurry. Calm is not an absence of life but life that doesn't need to prove its worth. You can simply allow it to yourself.
calm.practice: Walk slowly for a few minutes along a familiar path — a yard, a street, a corridor — as if on Heidegger's country path, letting your breath fall in with your step. Don't think about tasks; just walk.

inspiration.text: In the forest the painter André Marchand more than once felt that it was not he who looked at the trees but the trees that looked at him — Merleau-Ponty quotes this in “Eye and Mind.” Inspiration is a joyful and mysterious state, and it's worth cherishing. In the essay “Eye and Mind,” Merleau-Ponty wrote that the painter changes the world into paintings “by lending his body to the world”: inspiration is not a thought handed down from above but an exchange between the body and the world. Inspiration is neither a merit nor an accident but a moment when you are especially open to what surrounds you. There's no need to hold on to it by force: you can simply follow it and pay attention to what it shows you.
inspiration.practice: Don't write down the whole idea — just the first image or phrase that came. Let it be a beginning, not a finished result.

schadenfreude.text: Are we falling behind, catching up, getting ahead? Heidegger noticed that, living among others, we are almost unknowingly always checking this distance. That small glee at someone else's failure is awkward to notice in yourself, but it's very human and says nothing final about you. He called this feature of everyday “being-with-others” distantiality. Schadenfreude is a flash of relief within this endless comparing: someone else's fall shrinks, for a moment, the distance that was tormenting us. It's less malice than weariness with the comparison we're all drawn into. Once you notice this, you can loosen your grip a little: your life doesn't have to be measured by its distance from others.
schadenfreude.practice: Ask yourself: “Whom am I always measuring my distance against?” Imagine for a minute that this ruler doesn't exist.

contempt.text: We pass each other by, and the other “doesn't concern us” — this is how Heidegger described the “deficient” modes of solicitude, the most ordinary ones in everyday life. Contempt is a cold feeling, it isn't easy to admit in yourself, and there's no need to rush to judge yourself for it. Merleau-Ponty would add that we perceive another person first of all with the body — through gestures, gait, intonation — and understand them long before we have time to think. Perhaps contempt is a way of pushing someone away, making them “none of my concern,” most often because something in them did touch us after all. Ask not “who is this person?” but “what in me responded to their gesture?”
contempt.practice: Recall exactly which gesture, tone or act made you feel contempt. Name what it touched in you.

disgust.text: The body, for Merleau-Ponty, “understands” the world before any reasoning: it knows at once what to reach for and what to recoil from. This is a very bodily feeling, and there's no reason to be ashamed of it. Disgust is one such instant bodily meaning. When it's aimed at a situation or at people, it's the body saying “I can't be here.” When it's aimed at yourself, perhaps you're looking at your body from the outside, as an object, rather than living in it. Merleau-Ponty distinguished the “object-body,” which is looked at, from the “lived body,” through which we live. You can return to your body from the inside, rather than only judging it from the outside.
disgust.practice: Close your eyes and feel your feet, your palms, your breathing from the inside — not how you look, but how you are. For one minute.

revenge.text: “It was” — reading Nietzsche, Heidegger saw in revenge the will's aversion to precisely these two words. If you've been hurt and a force demanding justice is rising inside you, the wish for revenge is understandable. In his lecture “Who Is Nietzsche's Zarathustra?”, Heidegger examines Nietzsche's idea of the “spirit of revenge.” On his reading, revenge at bottom is the will's aversion to time and its “it was”: we can't change the past, and this powerlessness looks for an outlet by taking itself out on someone. The wish for revenge is not cruelty but torment over a past that can't be undone. This helps you see that no revenge will undo what happened. But you can look for ways to live with that “it was”: protecting yourself, seeking justice, giving the pain time.
revenge.practice: Say quietly to yourself: “It happened” — and breathe out slowly, adding no judgements and no plans. Then decide what's most needed now: to protect yourself, to seek justice, or to give the pain time.

anger_at_loved.text: A mood, Heidegger wrote, “assails” us: we don't choose it, we find ourselves already inside it, and it colours the whole world. When anger at loved ones flares up and shame follows, remember: you are not a bad person. Often we bring home a mood that formed somewhere else — and then any small thing a loved one does flares up in that light. Merleau-Ponty would add that with family we live in a shared bodily space: their movements, voices and habits constantly touch us, and a tired body reacts before we have time to think. An outburst is not the truth about your love but about your mood and your tiredness.
anger_at_loved.practice: After an outburst, ask: “What mood was I in before this even happened?” Name it in one word.

ambivalence.text: Merleau-Ponty touched his left hand with his right and noticed that you can't be both touching and touched at once — the feeling keeps switching. Loving someone and not being able to stand them is like that: hard, but very human. Merleau-Ponty's philosophy is sometimes called a “philosophy of ambiguity.” He showed that ambiguity is not an error of thinking but the very fabric of experience: our body both sees and is seen, we are both inside the world and looking at it, meaning is never finally clear. Heidegger, for his part, believed that care for another can take different forms, and they often intertwine. Mixed feelings towards someone close are not a sign of fake love but the natural many-sidedness of living relationships. You don't have to untangle the knot right away. You can simply acknowledge that it's there.
ambivalence.practice: Put your palms together so that one touches the other, and feel the sensation switching. Say quietly: “I love you, and it's hard for me to be with you” — and notice that both parts are true.

guilty_relief.text: Life, for Heidegger, doesn't simply go on — it has to be carried: moods disclose our existence to us as a “burden.” If after a break-up, a departure or a loved one's long illness you feel relief and guilt about it, know this: relief doesn't cancel love. When you carried someone else's illness, a difficult relationship, sleepless nights for a long time, that burden wasn't a metaphor but your everyday being. Relief is not betrayal but simply a change in the mood through which the world is disclosed: the weight has eased, and the body has felt it. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that the body knows its tiredness before our thoughts do. You can allow yourself both to breathe out and to grieve — one doesn't cancel the other.
guilty_relief.practice: Sit comfortably and feel where in your body things have become lighter. Tell yourself: “I carried a lot. I'm allowed to breathe out.”

indifference.text: In Being and Time Heidegger noticed something remarkable: even a flat, colourless lack of mood, when nothing touches you, is also a mood, not an absence of feeling. If where something “should” move you there's silence inside, it's frightening, but it doesn't make you heartless. We are always attuned somehow; it's just that sometimes the mood is grey and quiet. And it, too, discloses something: tiredness, for example, or that the world has moved back for a while. Indifference is not a hole in you but the way the world is given to you right now. You don't have to force yourself to feel “correctly.” You can describe this silence attentively, and describing it sometimes changes it by itself.
indifference.practice: Describe your indifference out loud in three words, like the weather: what colour, weight and temperature is it?

escape.text: “The done thing” — in Heidegger, the impersonal “das Man” quietly decides for us how to live and obscures our own possibilities. The urge to drop everything and leave — your job, your city, your role — says a lot in itself. Heidegger would take it seriously. Sometimes, he wrote, a “call of conscience” sounds — not the voice of morality, but a quiet summons back to yourself, to what you actually could be. The urge to run away isn't necessarily flight from yourself; sometimes it is exactly such a call. But it rarely demands that you destroy everything at once. Heidegger spoke of “projecting” possibilities: first you can simply see them and look at them closely.
escape.practice: Write: “What part of me can't be seen in my current role?” Don't decide anything — just take a close look.

forbidden_attraction.text: Desire, for Merleau-Ponty, is neither a thought nor an instinct but a way the body is turned towards another: it creates a particular atmosphere around a person that's hard to put into words. Attraction to someone who is “off-limits” can be unsettling and frightening, but the feeling itself decides nothing yet and doesn't make you bad. Such meaning arises before reasoning, so we can't simply “cancel” it by deciding to. You can approach the attraction with curiosity: what exactly does this person open up for you — aliveness, recognition, another version of yourself? Understanding the meaning of a feeling doesn't mean acting on it. It means knowing your own life better.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Picture this person and ask what the world becomes near them: brighter, more anxious, freer? Name one word to yourself and think where else in your life there's room for it.

social_anxiety.text: Under someone else's gaze, Merleau-Ponty noticed, the body stiffens: movements that usually flow by themselves suddenly have to be thought through. Fear of people and their judgement is exhausting, and you're not alone in it. Heidegger would explain whom we're really afraid of. Heidegger described the impersonal “das Man” — “the they,” “the done thing”: an anonymous authority that tells you how to look, talk and carry yourself. Often we're afraid not of a specific person but of this invisible “everyone.” Your shyness is the body's natural response to anonymous judgement. But Heidegger noted that this “everyone” is no one in particular. Sometimes it helps to come back from “what will people think” to the specific person in front of you, who is most likely a little nervous too.
social_anxiety.practice: Before a meeting, replace the thought “what will everyone think” with the question: “Who exactly will be there — and what do I know about them?”

quote.text: Everyone is the other, and no one is himself.
quote.author: Martin Heidegger

uncertainty.text: “We are condemned to meaning,” Merleau-Ponty wrote: however unclear the world is, we can't be left entirely without meaning. Uncertainty is draining: you want something to hold on to, and there's nothing. Heidegger described the human situation through two concepts. “Thrownness”: we have always already landed in a situation we didn't choose and can't fully survey. “Projection”: we live on nonetheless, reaching towards possibilities without knowing for sure which will come true. Uncertainty is not a malfunction but the basic structure of life, usually obscured by familiar plans. Meaning keeps taking shape in our experience. You don't have to wait for complete clarity; you can look for meaning in the next small step.
uncertainty.practice: Name one thing you're sure of right now — even the simplest: the cup in your hand, the floor under your feet.

quote.text: Because we are in the world, we are condemned to meaning.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

waiting.text: The late Heidegger wrote a conversation on a country path in which a scientist, a scholar and a teacher arrive at a strange thought: one can wait without knowing for what. When waiting for results, an answer or news stretches out agonisingly, there is relief in that thought. In that conversation, “Towards an Explication of Releasement,” he distinguished two kinds of waiting. One is a tense awaiting of something definite: we fasten onto the future, and the present becomes an empty corridor. The other is an open waiting that doesn't cling to a particular outcome and lets things come as they will. He linked this stance with “releasement” — a calm allowing of what is not in our power. What makes waiting agonising is often that we hold the future too tightly. Without ceasing to hope, you can loosen your grip a little and notice what is happening now.
waiting.practice: Unclench your fists, drop your shoulders, and for three minutes simply listen to the sounds around you, expecting nothing from them.

regret.text: In choosing one possibility, we inevitably leave others behind: for Heidegger this is not a personal mistake but the very structure of human life — no one can live out all their possibilities. If regret over something done or left undone won't let go, it shows what matters to you. It hurts, and it's an honest pain. Moreover, for Heidegger the past is neither closed nor dead: we go on carrying it, and its meaning changes depending on how we live on. Your regret is not a verdict but a sign that the past is still taking part in your life. You decide what it will become as things continue.
regret.practice: Finish: “Back then I didn't choose…, but the fact that it mattered to me I can keep like this: …”

longing.text: The world, for Heidegger, is always arranged together with others — and when one person disappears from it, a whole place in the world goes empty. If you miss one particular person, there's nothing shameful in it. Merleau-Ponty described the “phantom limb” in detail: after a loss, the body goes on feeling an arm or a leg and still reaches out to the world through it. There's something similar in longing: for years your world was arranged with this person in it — their voice in the evenings, their place at the table, a shared rhythm. Your body and habits keep reaching for them. This is the memory of your whole life. Longing gradually changes its shape as the world slowly rearranges itself, and there's no need to hurry it.
longing.practice: Notice one place or moment of the day where this person's absence is felt most strongly. Spend some time there, gently.

world_pain.text: “But where danger is, grows the saving power also” — the late Heidegger quoted these lines of Hölderlin in “The Question Concerning Technology.” If hard news, violence and injustice hurt you, it speaks of your capacity for compassion. Heidegger believed human beings are always “being-with-others”: even distant people are part of our world, and their suffering concerns us. The late Heidegger reflected a great deal on the dangers of the age. You can avoid turning away from the pain without drowning in it either. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that what we lean on is always bodily and concrete: people close to us, the ground under our feet, small good deeds. The world's pain is easier to carry when you're holding on to something nearby.
world_pain.practice: Put the news aside and read Hölderlin's line aloud: “But where danger is, grows the saving power also.” Then name five things around you and decide on one good thing you can do close by.

quote.text: But where danger is, grows the saving power also.
quote.author: Friedrich Hölderlin
quote.source: the hymn “Patmos”; quoted by Heidegger in “The Question Concerning Technology” (1953)

rejection.text: A gaze, a tone, a withdrawn gesture get inside us before we can make sense of them — that is how Merleau-Ponty described our bodily openness to others. So when you are rejected — for a job, a friendship, a love — the refusal wounds deeply and can feel like a blow, a tightness in the chest, a wish to hide. That is natural: the body responds honestly. Heidegger would add that “being-with-others” is part of our very structure: we are open to others, and therefore vulnerable. Your pain is the price of this openness. One refusal doesn't cancel the fact that you exist among many people. You can let your body feel the blow — and then slowly take back your space.
rejection.practice: Call someone today around whom you feel accepted — just to talk. One refusal doesn't cancel the fact that you exist among many people.

abandonment.text: Heidegger noticed a paradox: even loneliness is a way of being with others, since you can only miss someone who could be there. If you're afraid of being left, it's a deep feeling, and it deserves gentleness. Heidegger wrote that a human being is by their very nature “being-with”: we always live in a world shared with others. This fear is a sharp sense of how much we are woven from connections. Merleau-Ponty spoke of “intercorporeality” — the bodily intertwining of people with one another. The fear shows how much the people close to you mean to you. And it also reminds you that connection doesn't rest on one person: you are woven into a whole web.
abandonment.practice: Name five people or places you are connected with — even loosely. Picture these threads for a minute.

unrequited.text: To “leap in” for another or to “leap ahead” — Heidegger distinguished two forms of care: one takes over for the other and manages them, the other helps them be free in their own possibilities. If you love without being loved back, your pain is real. Heidegger helps you see more in it than a wound. The most caring love recognises the other's freedom, including their freedom not to answer. This doesn't make the pain smaller, but it gives your love dignity: you loved a person rather than trying to possess them. Merleau-Ponty would remind us that love lives in the body, and it needs time to change its shape.
unrequited.practice: Read aloud slowly: “I let you be free. And I allow myself to grieve.”

humiliation.text: Who is looking here, and who is being looked at? A phenomenologist would begin a conversation about humiliation with this question. It is one of the most painful experiences, and it isn't your fault that you went through it. Merleau-Ponty described the body as something that both sees and is seen. In humiliation this balance breaks: it's as if you've been turned into an object put on display under someone else's gaze, and stripped of the role of the one who looks. Heidegger would call this the power of the impersonal “das Man,” which seems to pass a verdict in the name of “everyone.” Humiliation is not the truth about you but a situation in which you were deprived of the position of a subject. You can take it back gradually: begin once more to see, to act, to speak in the first person.
humiliation.practice: Look around and name out loud three things you see. You are once again the one who looks.

body_shame.text: “We don't have a body; we are a body” — this thought of Merleau-Ponty's is easy to say and hard to live. If you're unhappy with your body, it's a very common and painful feeling. Merleau-Ponty distinguished the body looked at as an object — something that can be measured and judged — from the “lived body” through which we live: through which we see, touch, move, embrace. Body shame is when we start living only the first, constantly looking at ourselves from the outside, as if in a mirror. You can little by little return to your body from the inside: not how it looks, but what it lets you feel and do. It is not a project to be corrected but your way of being in the world.
body_shame.practice: Make one simple movement — stretch, walk a little — and pay attention only to how it feels from the inside, not to how it looks.

illness.text: For a blind man, Merleau-Ponty wrote, the cane stops being an object: he feels the world at its tip, as an extension of his hand. When your body is ill and lets you down, the whole world changes, and that's hard. Merleau-Ponty wrote that consciousness is originally not an “I think” but an “I can”: we live the world through the body's possibilities — to reach, to walk somewhere, to lift. When the body is ill, the world changes: stairs become an obstacle, the street becomes far away. Your distress is understandable: you're losing not only strength but also your familiar world. But Merleau-Ponty also showed that the body is capable of rebuilding its “I can,” of finding new ways of being in the world. You can gently look for these new possibilities — however small they may be.
illness.practice: Name one “I can” you have today — even the smallest. Stay with it for a while.

quote.text: The body is our general medium for having a world.
quote.author: Maurice Merleau-Ponty

pride.text: A cabinetmaker's apprentice, Heidegger said, learns not tricks but responsiveness to wood — to the shapes slumbering within it. When a skill like that becomes yours, pride in what you've done is a healthy and deserved feeling. Merleau-Ponty showed that consciousness is originally an “I can,” and that every skill mastered becomes part of the body. Pride is the moment when your “I can” has taken form and become visible: this has been done, and I did it. It isn't boasting or comparison with others, but joy in a world that has grown wider. Let yourself stay with this feeling. Perhaps you'll notice that you're holding yourself differently right now — straighter, freer.
pride.practice: Look at what you've made and notice how you're standing or sitting. Let yourself stay in that posture for a minute.

melancholy.text: “Philosophy is really homesickness, an urge to be at home everywhere” — Heidegger opened his course The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics with these words of Novalis. A quiet sadness, sorrow mixed with tenderness, is akin to that homesickness, and it doesn't need to be “fixed.” Heidegger regarded moods not as random emotions but as ways in which the world is disclosed. Melancholy is a mood in which the world is disclosed in its fragility and depth: we feel how everything passes, and precisely for that reason we see how precious it is. Melancholy doesn't weaken but deepens: in it you seem closer to something essential. Allow yourself to stay in it, without hurrying to chase it away.
melancholy.practice: Read Novalis's line aloud: “Philosophy is really homesickness.” Then spend five minutes by a window or with music and simply let this mood be.

quote.text: Philosophy is really homesickness, an urge to be at home everywhere.
quote.author: Novalis
quote.source: quoted by Heidegger in The Fundamental Concepts of Metaphysics (1929–1930)
